title: ABSTRACT ALGEBRA
body:
The course that stops asking what things *are* and starts asking what they *do*. Take a set, name
the operations on it, list the rules those operations obey, and then prove everything you can from
the rules alone: whatever you prove holds for every system obeying them, forever. The structures
climb in one direction, each adding a requirement to the one before, [[Group]] to [[Ring]] to
[[Field]], and the course is the story of what each addition buys. It starts concretely with the
[[Integer]]s, congruences, and [[Modular Arithmetic]], because $\mathbb{Z}$ is the example every
later abstraction is modelled on, and it finishes at [[Finite Field|finite fields]], which is where
the abstraction turns back into something a machine can run.

It is the same axiomatic move [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] makes with [[Vector Space]], and that course
predicts this one explicitly. It is also the vault's tightest prerequisite chain: [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]]
(MATH 4111) lists MATH 2101 as its prerequisite and spends its whole term using the groups, rings,
and finite fields built here. The [[Cyclic Group]] structure of the [[Roots of Unity]] is what the
[[Discrete Fourier Transform]] is built from in [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]], and $GF(2^8)$ is
why arithmetic on a [[Byte]] is a field at all.

## Topics

### Number theory, and the third rung of a ladder

The same objects [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] writes as C++ exercises and
[[DISCRETE MATH]] proves theorems about, taken a third time as **structure**.

- [[Modular Arithmetic]] is the hub: congruence classes, $\mathbb{Z}_n$, linear congruences, and
  modular exponentiation. The remainder stops being a value you compute and becomes a name for a
  class of [[Integer]]s.
- [[Euclidean Algorithm]] computes $\gcd$, and its extended form produces Bézout's identity, which
  is the only general way to invert an element mod $n$. [[GCD and LCM]] has the implementation;
  this note has the proof, the termination argument, and the $O(\log n)$ claim.
- [[Division Algorithm]] and [[Prime Number]] are the first-year notes this block builds on. What
  changes here is the reading: the gcd is a generator, primality is irreducibility, and
  $\mathbb{Z}_n$ is a quotient [[Ring]].

### Groups

One set, one operation, four axioms, and a surprising amount of consequence.

- [[Group]] carries the axioms, the elementary properties (uniqueness of identity and inverses,
  cancellation, $(ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1}$), and the table of what is and is not a group.
- [[Subgroup]] is a group inside a group, plus the one-step test that saves you checking the
  axioms again.
- [[Cyclic Group]] is generated by a single element, and there are only two of them up to
  relabelling: $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}_n$. This is the note the rest of the vault actually
  reaches for.

### Permutations and symmetry

The concrete groups, and by Cayley's theorem also the general case.

- [[Permutation Group]] covers cycle notation, why the parity of a permutation is well defined,
  and Cayley's theorem: every finite group is a permutation group in disguise.
- [[Symmetric Group]] is $S_n$, all $n!$ of them, and the smallest non-abelian example lives here
  as $S_3$.
- [[Alternating Group]] is the even half, $A_n$, of order $n!/2$.
- [[Dihedral Group]] is $D_n$, the $2n$ symmetries of a regular $n$-gon, and it is the example to
  hold in your hands: the relation $srs = r^{-1}$ *is* non-commutativity written down.

### Cosets and the first real theorem

- [[Coset]] shifts a subgroup around the group, and the three facts (equal size, disjoint or
  identical, covering) partition $G$ into equal blocks.
- [[Lagrange's Theorem]] divides that partition out: $|H|$ divides $|G|$. Its corollaries are the
  order of an element dividing $|G|$, every group of prime order being cyclic, and Fermat's little
  theorem, which is where a purely structural result turns into the arithmetic RSA runs on.

### Maps between structures

- [[Homomorphism]] preserves the operation and is allowed to lose information;
  $\det$ and the sign of a permutation are the two examples already in the vault.
- [[Isomorphism]] loses none, so the two groups are the same thing wearing different labels. The
  useful skill is the opposite one: proving two groups are *not* isomorphic by finding an
  invariant they disagree on.

### Rings and polynomials

Two operations now, and the model is $\mathbb{Z}$ rather than a symmetry.

- [[Ring]] carries the axioms, the ladder from ring to commutative ring to integral domain to
  field, zero divisors as the thing that goes wrong, and ideals as what you quotient by.
  $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} = \mathbb{Z}_n$ is the example that ties the block back to block 1.
- [[Polynomial Ring]] is $F[x]$, and the whole section is the observation that it behaves almost
  exactly like $\mathbb{Z}$: division with remainder, a Euclidean algorithm, unique factorisation,
  and quotients. The remainder and factor theorems fall out in one line each.
- [[Irreducibility]] is primality for polynomials, and it depends on the field you stand in.
  Eisenstein, the rational root theorem, and the degree-2-or-3 shortcut are the tests.

### Fields and extensions

- [[Field]] is a commutative ring where division works: two abelian groups on one set. It carries
  the characteristic, which is always 0 or prime, and the reason so much of the degree quietly
  assumes one.
- [[Field Extension]] adjoins a root of an irreducible polynomial. $\mathbb{C} =
  \mathbb{R}[x]/(x^2+1)$ is the worked example, and it is the middle rung of the vault's
  complex-numbers ladder.
- [[Finite Field]] is where the course lands. Sizes are exactly the prime powers, there is exactly
  one of each size, and $GF(2^8)$ is the field a byte lives in. Alias: Galois field.

## Core Facts to Know

- A [[Group]] is closure, associativity, an identity, and inverses. **Commutativity is not an
  axiom**; a group that has it is called abelian.
- The identity and inverses are unique, cancellation holds, and $(ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1}$, order
  reversed.
- **Order** means two things: $|G|$, the number of elements, and the order of an element $a$, the
  smallest $k>0$ with $a^k = e$.
- A [[Subgroup]] needs only non-emptiness plus closure under the operation and under inverses.
  For a **finite** subset, closure alone is enough.
- Every [[Cyclic Group]] is abelian, and up to [[Isomorphism]] there are only two: $\mathbb{Z}$ and
  $\mathbb{Z}_n$. Not every abelian group is cyclic.
- $g^k$ generates $\langle g \rangle$ of order $n$ exactly when $\gcd(k,n) = 1$.
- The $n$th [[Roots of Unity]] are a cyclic group of order $n$ under multiplication: angles add and
  wrap, which is $\mathbb{Z}_n$ drawn on the unit circle.
- Every permutation factors into disjoint cycles, and its **order is the lcm of the cycle lengths**.
- **Parity is well defined**: every decomposition of a permutation into transpositions has the same
  parity. A $k$-cycle is even exactly when $k$ is odd.
- $|S_n| = n!$ and $|A_n| = n!/2$. $|D_n| = 2n$. $S_3 = D_3$ is the smallest non-abelian group.
- **Cayley: every finite group is isomorphic to a subgroup of some [[Symmetric Group]].**
- The left [[Coset|cosets]] of $H$ partition $G$ into disjoint blocks all of size $|H|$.
- **[[Lagrange's Theorem]]: $|H|$ divides $|G|$**, and $|G| = [G:H]\cdot|H|$. The converse is
  false: $A_4$ has order 12 and no subgroup of order 6.
- Corollary: the order of every element divides $|G|$, so $a^{|G|} = e$ for all $a$.
- Every group of prime order is cyclic and has no non-trivial subgroups.
- A [[Homomorphism]] satisfies $\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b)$ and need not be injective;
  **it is injective exactly when its kernel is trivial.**
- $a \equiv b \pmod n$ means $n \mid (a-b)$. Congruence survives $+$ and $\times$, so you may
  reduce at any point in a calculation. It does **not** survive cancellation.
- $[a]$ is invertible in $\mathbb{Z}_n$ exactly when $\gcd(a,n) = 1$, and the extended
  [[Euclidean Algorithm]] is how you find the inverse.
- The Euclidean algorithm is $O(\log \min(a,b))$ divisions, with consecutive Fibonacci numbers as
  the worst case.
- **Bézout: $\gcd(a,b) = ax + by$ for some integers $x,y$.** Structurally, the gcd generates the
  ideal that $a$ and $b$ generate.
- A [[Ring]] is an abelian group under $+$, a monoid-ish structure under $\times$, and
  distributive. **Commutativity, a 1, and inverses are all optional.**
- A **zero divisor** is a non-zero $a$ with $ab = 0$ for some non-zero $b$. An **integral domain**
  has none, which is exactly what makes cancellation legal.
- **$\mathbb{Z}_n$ is a [[Field]] if and only if $n$ is prime.** Otherwise $n = ab$ gives zero
  divisors.
- $\mathbb{Z}$ is the integral domain that is not a field, and that gap is where all of
  divisibility and factorisation lives.
- $\operatorname{char}(F)$ is 0 or a prime. In characteristic 2, $x + x = 0$, so addition is XOR
  and subtraction is addition.
- In $F[x]$: $\deg(fg) = \deg f + \deg g$, division with remainder works, $(x-a) \mid f$ exactly
  when $f(a) = 0$, and a degree-$n$ polynomial has at most $n$ roots.
- $F[x]/(f)$ is a field exactly when $f$ is [[Irreducibility|irreducible]], the same statement as
  $\mathbb{Z}_p$ being a field one level down.
- **Irreducibility depends on the field.** $x^2+1$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{R}$ and splits over
  $\mathbb{C}$. Degree 2 or 3 is reducible iff it has a root; **that test fails from degree 4**.
- $[K:F]$, the degree of an extension, is the dimension of $K$ as a [[Vector Space]] over $F$, and
  equals $\deg f$ when you adjoin a root of $f$. $[\mathbb{C}:\mathbb{R}] = 2$.
- **A [[Finite Field]] has $p^n$ elements, a prime power, and there is exactly one of each size.**
  $\mathbb{Z}_4$ is *not* a field; $GF(4) = \mathbb{Z}_2[x]/(x^2+x+1)$ is.
- The non-zero elements of a finite field form a cyclic group of order $q-1$.
- $GF(2^8)$ is a [[Byte]]: addition is XOR, multiplication is carry-less multiply then reduce mod a
  fixed irreducible degree-8 polynomial. Every non-zero byte has an inverse, which is what AES and
  Reed-Solomon are built on.

## Related courses

- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTER SCIENCE 2]] (COMP 1633) owns the **implementations** of block 1.
  [[Division Algorithm]] is `/` and `%`, [[GCD and LCM]] is Euclid as a `while` loop and the first
  [[Recursion]] example, [[Prime Number]] is trial division stopping at $\sqrt{n}$. This course
  supplies the reason each of them is correct.
- [[DISCRETE MATH]] (MATH 1271) is the middle rung: [[Proof]], [[Proof By Induction]], and
  [[Sets]] are the tools this course assumes, and its number theory is where existence and
  uniqueness get proved. **Watch the homograph**: [[Permutation]] there is a *count*, $P(n,r)$;
  [[Permutation Group]] here is an *object*, and $n!$ is where the two meet.
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] (MATH 1203) makes the same axiomatic move one structure over. [[Vector Space]]
  says so out loud, and a vector space is defined **over a field**, so [[Field]] is the missing
  half of that definition. [[Complex Numbers]] there is $\mathbb{R}$ with a root of $x^2+1$
  adjoined here; [[Determinant]] is a [[Homomorphism]]; [[Kernel and Range]] is the same theorem as
  kernel and image.
- [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]] (MATH 4111) has this course as its stated prerequisite and it shows. RSA is
  [[Modular Arithmetic]] plus Fermat plus [[Euclidean Algorithm|modular inversion]], AES is
  arithmetic in $GF(2^8)$, Diffie-Hellman is the discrete logarithm in a [[Cyclic Group]], and
  elliptic curves are a group law on a curve over a [[Finite Field]]. Three of that course's
  foundations are written here.
- [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] (MATH 4199) is where [[Cyclic Group]] pays off outside algebra.
  The [[Roots of Unity]] form one, the [[Discrete Fourier Transform]] matrix is built from powers
  of a single generator, and the [[Fast Fourier Transform]]'s halving step is passing to the
  order-$n/2$ subgroup.
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]] (COMP 2655) and [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] (COMP 2659) are doing this
  algebra in hardware without naming it. [[Integer Representation]] and [[Complements]] are
  arithmetic in $\mathbb{Z}_{2^n}$, so unsigned overflow is reduction working correctly rather than
  a fault. [[Boolean Algebra]] is $GF(2)$ from the circuit side, and [[Error Detection]]'s parity
  bit is a linear equation over it.
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] (COMP 2631) uses $\mathbb{Z}_n$ every time it hashes.
  [[Hashing]] and [[Hash Function]] map a key to a congruence class, and the standard advice to
  take a prime table size is this course's theorem about $\mathbb{Z}_p$.
- [[ALGORITHMS AND COMPLEXITY]] gets the [[Euclidean Algorithm]] as the canonical logarithmic
  algorithm, and $|S_n| = n!$ as the reason brute force over orderings is hopeless: see
  [[Hamiltonian Cycle]], [[Time Complexity]], and the $\Omega(n\log n)$ sorting bound in
  [[Sequential Sorting]], which counts the same $n!$ a different way.
- [[INTRODUCTION TO COMPUTABILITY]] (COMP 2613) shares the idea behind [[Isomorphism]]:
  [[Simulation]] is one machine imitating another, and "the same up to relabelling" is the strict
  version of it.
- [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]] (`Books/`) holds [[Error Correcting Code]], which is
  [[Finite Field]] theory applied. Reed-Solomon treats a block of bytes as a polynomial over
  $GF(2^8)$, and the at-most-$n$-roots fact from [[Polynomial Ring]] is why the redundancy works.
